problem_statement: The paper frames the problem as pricing European call options under uncertainty, where the asset price evolves randomly and the fair value must be estimated from simulated future paths. It also treats the broader task as a computational problem in option pricing that can be addressed with Monte Carlo simulation and, potentially, quantum Monte Carlo.
problem_statement_quotes: As one of the major methods for the simulation of option pricing, Monte Carlo method assumes random fluctuations in the distribution of asset prices.
Due to the randomness of the defined parameters, it is feasible but difficult to calculate the fair value [2].
This article mainly focuses on the application of MC and QMC methods in European call options and further analysis for the certain examples.
classical_baseline: The classical baseline is the standard Monte Carlo method for option pricing, which the paper describes as the commonly used numerical approach for European options. The paper also references the Black-Scholes(-Merton) framework as the pricing model underlying the option valuation setup.
classical_baseline_quotes: Many numerical methods, especially Monte Carlo (MC) method has been commonly used in pricing system due to its flexibility and ability to handle generically stochastic parameters [3,4].
The dominant advantage of MC method is that the error convergence rate does not depend on the dimensionality of the problem.

classical_difficulty: The paper says the classical Monte Carlo approach needs many simulations to achieve accurate pricing, which leads to huge and expensive calculations. It also states that option pricing generally requires tens of millions of simulations and a lot of time, even though the error convergence rate is dimension-independent.
